1 · Quick-Reference Practice Sheet

All 24 movements of the Simplified Form, standing and seated cues side by side, condensed directly from the book’s instructions.

Check with your doctor before starting, especially with pre-existing conditions. Stop and rest if you feel pain, dizziness, or shortness of breath.
#MovementStandingSeated
1Commencing FormRaise arms to shoulder height, then lower as knees settle.Arms float up to chest height, sink as you exhale.
2Part the Wild Horse's ManeStep out; front hand rises to eye height, back hand sinks.Extend leg forward; same-side hand rises, opposite hand sinks.
3White Crane Spreads Its WingsDraw foot in on toes; right hand arcs above forehead.Right hand rises above forehead, left hand settles near hip.
4Brush Knee and Twist StepStep forward; one hand brushes past knee, other pushes forward.Extend leg forward; same-side hand brushes knee, other pushes forward.
5Hand Strums the LuteWeight back, front heel down, hands meet like holding instrument.Both hands meet at chest, one higher, weight settles evenly.
6Step Back and Repulse MonkeyStep backward; one hand draws to ear, other pushes forward.Shift into chair back; draw one hand back, push other forward.
7Left Grasp the Bird's TailWard off, roll back, press, push, weight and torso turning.Same four arm actions; weight shifts gently between hips.
8Right Grasp the Bird's TailRepeat ward off, roll back, press, push, mirrored to the right.Same four connected actions, mirrored, weight shifting hip to hip.
9Single WhipWide stance, weight on one leg, other arm hooks out fully.Extend one arm into hook shape, weight settles on that hip.
10Wave Hands Like CloudsSide-step slowly, hands circle as weight rocks side to side.Both hands rise to chest height; torso turns slowly side to side.
11Single Whip (repeated)Repeat the wide hook-hand stance from movement nine.Repeat the seated hook-hand version from movement nine.
12High Pat on HorseWeight fully back; one hand draws to ear, one extends palm-up.One hand draws back near ear, other extends forward, palm up.
13Kick with Right HeelExtend leg slowly, heel leading; keep standing leg grounded.Extend one leg forward slowly, heel leading, toes lifted.
14Strike Ears with Both FistsFists arc inward and up beside head as weight shifts forward.Curl fists, arc them up beside head, weight settles forward slightly.
15Turn and Kick with Left HeelPivot to change direction, then mirror the heel kick left.Extend one leg forward slowly, heel leading, toes lifted.
16Left Lower Body and Stand on One Leg (Golden Rooster)Lower body, then stand on one leg; knee lifts to hip height.Lift knee toward chest, hold a breath or two, lower slowly.
17Right Lower Body and Stand on One Leg (Golden Rooster)Mirror to the other side; stand rooted, knee lifts to hip height.Repeat on the other side: lift knee, hold, lower with control.
18Fair Lady Works the ShuttlesTravel to a corner; one hand guards forehead, other pushes out.One hand guards forehead, other pushes out, torso turns to diagonal.
19Needle at Sea BottomFold forward from hips; one hand draws down toward floor.Fold forward gently, keeping the motion small and comfortable.
20Flash the ArmOne arm sweeps up to protect head, other pushes forward.Sweep one arm up and out, other pushes forward, torso opens.
21Turn, Deflect, Parry and PunchSmall defensive hand moves, then a slow, controlled forward punch.Same defensive moves and slow punch; torso turns instead of stepping.
22Apparent Close UpHands draw to chest, then push forward as weight shifts forward.Draw hands to chest, push forward, weight settles back then forward.
23Cross HandsFeet return to shoulder width; hands cross in front of chest.Feet flat and even; hands cross in front of chest.
24Closing FormHands separate, lower slowly to sides as weight settles evenly.Hands float up, then sink slowly to rest on thighs.

3 · Your 30-Day Practice Program

A starting template, not a prescription — the same honest approach as the two-week calendar in Chapter 7, stretched out further. Foundation work in week one, the first half of the Simplified 24-Form in weeks two and three, the second half in week four, and a review in the final days. Two days a week are deliberately not tai chi days. Swap in whichever postures you've actually learned so far — the point is the rhythm, not keeping exact pace with the calendar.

Week 1 · Foundation

DaySessionLength
1Warm-up + basic stance (Chapter 4)10 min
2Warm-up + weight-shift drill10 min
3Warm-up + Commencing Form10 min
4Rest or gentle walk instead of tai chi—
5Warm-up + Commencing Form, slightly slower12 min
6Warm-up + basic stance + weight-shift review12 min
7Warm-up + full review of the week, standing or seated as needed12 min

Week 2 · Movements 1 Through 8

DaySessionLength
8Warm-up + Commencing Form + Part the Wild Horse's Mane12 min
9Warm-up + seated equivalent of Day 812 min
10Warm-up + White Crane Spreads Its Wings (add to Day 8)15 min
11Rest or gentle stretching instead of tai chi—
12Warm-up + Brush Knee and Twist Step (add to sequence)15 min
13Warm-up + full review, seated12 min
14Warm-up + Hand Strums the Lute + Step Back and Repulse Monkey15 min

Week 3 · Movements 9 Through 16

DaySessionLength
15Warm-up + Left and Right Grasp the Bird's Tail15 min
16Warm-up + seated equivalent of Day 1512 min
17Rest or gentle walk instead of tai chi—
18Warm-up + Single Whip + Wave Hands Like Clouds15 min
19Warm-up + High Pat on Horse (add to sequence)15 min
20Warm-up + whichever section felt least steady this week, repeated slowly15 min
21Warm-up + full review, standing or seated15 min

Week 4 · Movements 17 Through 24

DaySessionLength
22Warm-up + Kick with Right Heel + Strike Ears with Both Fists15 min
23Rest or gentle stretching instead of tai chi—
24Warm-up + Turn and Kick with Left Heel + Golden Rooster15 min
25Warm-up + seated equivalent of Day 2412 min
26Warm-up + Fair Lady Works the Shuttles + Needle at Sea Bottom15 min
27Rest or gentle walk instead of tai chi—
28Warm-up + Flash the Arm + Turn, Deflect, Parry and Punch15 min

Days 29–30 · Bringing It Together

DaySessionLength
29Warm-up + Apparent Close Up + Cross Hands + Closing Form15 min
30Warm-up + full sequence review, standing or seated, at whatever pace feels steady15–20 min

If you practice on twenty to twenty-two days out of these thirty, the program has done its job — the same honest math the rest of this book uses. A short session repeated often adds up to more than a perfect streak chased and then abandoned.

4 · Printable 30-Day Habit Tracker

A simple paper tracker, the same idea described in Chapter 8: a date, a checkmark, and one honest word about how the session felt — steady, rushed, off-balance, calm. Print it and keep it somewhere you'll actually see it: the refrigerator, next to the coffee maker, on a nightstand. A week of checkmarks is modest evidence, but it's evidence you produced yourself.

5 · Printable Glossary Card

Every tai chi term used in the book, in one place — sourced word for word from the back of the book. Print it and keep it nearby the first few times a term comes up mid-practice.

Brush Knee and Twist Step — a standing posture in the Simplified 24-Form in which the practitioner steps forward while one hand sweeps down and past the knee and the other pushes forward at shoulder height.
Cheng Man-ch'ing's 37 Postures — a 37-posture shortened form of Yang style, created by Cheng Man-ch'ing in mainland China by the mid-1940s, brought to Taiwan in 1949 and later to the United States in the 1960s; kept distinct in this book from the Simplified 24-Form.
Commencing Form — the opening movement of the Simplified 24-Form, also called the Preparation Form, that introduces the coordination of rising and lowering arms with bending knees.
Dan tien — a traditional focal point located roughly one to two inches below the navel, used to direct attention and initiate movement; presented in the book as traditional teaching, not as a measurable anatomical structure.
Empty leg — the leg carrying little to none of the practitioner's weight during a posture, left free to step, shift, or extend.
Golden Rooster Stands on One Leg — a standing posture in which one leg supports the full body weight while the other knee lifts to roughly hip height, described in traditional teaching as rooted.
Grasp the Bird's Tail — a posture appearing in various forms throughout the Simplified 24-Form, moving through four connected actions: ward off, roll back, press, and push.
Grounding — a traditional term, used interchangeably with “rooted,” for the sense of a stable stance connected through the standing leg into the floor.
Part the Wild Horse's Mane — an early posture in the Simplified 24-Form in which the practitioner steps out to the side while the hands separate, as though parting an imaginary ball held at the hip.
Rooted / Rootedness — traditional language for a stable, connected stance in which weight settles fully through the standing leg into the ground, rather than sitting rigidly on top of the joints.
Seated tai chi — tai chi practiced from a chair instead of standing; presented throughout the book as an equally legitimate, complete form of practice rather than a modified or lesser version.
Simplified 24-Form — a standardized 24-movement sequence, drawn primarily from Yang style, created in 1956 by a committee under China's national sports authority for mass public health use; also called the Beijing Form, the 24-Posture Form, or Simplified Taijiquan.
Single Whip — a posture in which the practitioner extends into a wide stance with weight almost entirely on one leg while the opposite arm extends fully to the side into a relaxed “hook hand.”
Taijiquan — the formal Chinese name for tai chi; the book notes the Simplified 24-Form is also called “Simplified Taijiquan.”
Wave Hands Like Clouds — a posture in which the hands trace slow, circular paths in front of the body while the weight shifts rhythmically from side to side; often described by practitioners as one of the calmest movements in the form.
Weight-bearing leg — the leg currently holding most of the practitioner's weight during a posture or weight shift.
Yang style — the tai chi tradition developed by Yang Luchan in the early-to-mid 1800s, adapted from the Chen family's martial art into smoother, more evenly paced movement; the source tradition for the Simplified 24-Form taught in this book.
